strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine gap in video understanding benchmarks where chain-of-thought reasoning benefits have not been demonstrated
Principled task formalization: Elegant state transition framework with clear three-level reasoning taxonomy (recall, infer, predict)
Comprehensive benchmark design: Six diverse video types, balanced distribution across skills, semi-automatic construction pipeline, detailed prompt templates
Thorough evaluation: 18 SOTA models tested with human baseline at 73.8%, ablation studies on thinking budget and visual inputs, integration into VLMEvalKit

Important empirical findings: Demonstrates thinking is essential for complex video reasoning (18.8%→27.4% improvement) while providing minimal benefits on existing benchmarks, reveals high visual dependence
Strong visual robustness analysis: Shows 55% performance drop when removing 50% frames vs. <7% on other benchmarks, validating vision-centric design
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Benchmark-only contribution without proposed methods; task formalization is competent but straightforward; no solutions for practitioners
Modest dataset scale: 1,440 questions with only 40 videos per category is small by modern standards; no clear train/val/test split specified
Heavy reliance on synthetic data: 4 out of 6 video types are synthetic (66%); only 2 real-world categories (Card, Chip) with limited diversity; unclear generalization to naturalistic video reasoning

Evaluation methodology concerns: Single judge model (Qwen2.5-72B) for all LLM-based evaluation introduces bias risk; human baseline on only 17% of data with no inter-annotator agreement reported; free-form correctness judgment reliability unclear

Incomplete analysis: No qualitative error analysis or failure case studies; thinking patterns not analyzed beyond token counts; missing ablations on prompt design; limited investigation of model-specific strengths/weaknesses
Contextual confounds: Long videos (avg 54.3s, max 154.8s) and extended prompts (avg 198.8 words) make it difficult to isolate reasoning limitations from context length constraints
Unclear differentiation from concurrent work: MINERVA and VCR-Bench mentioned but differences not clearly articulated; no cross-benchmark comparison to assess relative merit
Statistical rigor issues: No confidence intervals or significance testing; unclear if single-run or averaged results; small human baseline sample limits generalization

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap in video reasoning benchmarks that lack CoT depth
Principled three-level reasoning taxonomy (recall, infer, predict) with systematic difficulty progression
Comprehensive evaluation of 18 SOTA MLLMs with thorough ablation studies on video complexity, vision reliance, and state reveal timing
Diverse demonstration types (6 categories) reducing task-specific artifacts
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and useful human baseline providing context (73.8%)
Interesting finding that extended thinking is critical for this benchmark but offers minimal gains on existing ones (Figure 5)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applying existing state-transition reasoning frameworks to video is incremental; benchmark construction is straightforward procedural generation

Severe ecological validity concerns: 4 of 6 demonstrations are synthetic (Matplotlib, command-line); unclear if synthetic puzzles capture real video reasoning challenges vs. narrow symbolic manipulation
No qualitative error analysis or interpretability: no examples of successful vs. failed reasoning chains; unclear whether failures stem from visual perception, temporal tracking, or reasoning
Problematic evaluation methodology: using LLM (Qwen-72B) as judge without inter-rater reliability study; no exact-match baselines despite structured answers; binary correct/incorrect lacks nuance

Questionable 'vision-centric' framing: tasks are heavily logical/symbolic reasoning-dependent; Table 3 visual removal results don't disambiguate whether difficulty is from visual loss or information density
Weak human baseline: only 16.7% of dataset annotated; no inter-annotator agreement reported; substantial gap to model performance (73.8% vs 56%) raises reliability questions
Superficial analysis of thinking/CoT benefits: unclear whether improvements stem from computational budget or architectural differences; no sampling of actual reasoning chains
No constructive insights or improvement paths: paper explicitly lacks methods for performance improvement, limiting diagnostic value and practical utility
Poor statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars; appear to be single-run results with no variance analysis
Incomplete comparison with concurrent work: VCR-Bench and MINERVA dismissed in 2 sentences without quantitative comparative analysis

strengths: Well-motivated benchmark addressing genuine gap in video understanding evaluation—most existing benchmarks lack reasoning depth to showcase advantages of extended CoT reasoning
Thoughtful three-level reasoning framework (Recall→Infer→Predict) with clever state-based task design that forces genuine reasoning rather than surface pattern matching

Comprehensive evaluation of 18 SOTA models with strong ablations demonstrating benchmark uniqueness: 55% performance drop with 50% video removal (vs. <7% on others), 9% improvement with thinking budget (vs. <2.5% on others)
Clear presentation with informative figures, well-organized structure, detailed appendices enabling reproducibility and integration with VLMEvalKit
Diverse task design with six task categories spanning synthetic and real-world videos, providing good coverage of reasoning patterns
Rigorous evaluation methodology with both LLM-based evaluation and clever simulation-based verification for Predict Operation tasks
weaknesses: Tasks are somewhat artificial with deterministic state transitions and unambiguous answers—unclear how improvements transfer to real-world video understanding with subjective aspects
Limited human evaluation: only 240/1,440 examples (17%) evaluated; no inter-annotator agreement scores; no analysis of evaluation disagreement or ambiguous cases

Incomplete error analysis: no per-task-type breakdown, no detailed error categorization, surprisingly low Level 1 (Recall) performance <30% suggests fundamental vision issues deserving deeper analysis
Statistical rigor concerns: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars; single-run results without variance estimates; human baseline on only 17% of data limits generalizability
Only 2 of 6 task types use real-world videos; programmatically generated videos may not capture real video complexity (artifacts, lighting, motion blur)
Limited validation of LLM-based evaluation: no demonstrated correlation with human judgment; potential systematic biases from using Qwen2.5-72B as judge not addressed
Incomplete analysis of state reveal timing: substantial performance differences (45.1% vs 66.9%) with only 4 models evaluated; interaction with reasoning levels under-explored
Minimal comparison with concurrent related work (VCR-Bench, MINERVA); claims that these 'fall short' lack empirical support
Generalization concerns: all tasks involve discrete state tracking with deterministic answers; unclear coverage of diverse reasoning types needed for real-world video understanding

strengths: Clear and timely motivation: identifies genuine gap where existing video benchmarks lack reasoning depth to demonstrate extended CoT benefits
Principled and elegant benchmark design: state transition framework with partial visibility naturally induces reasoning difficulty, three-level hierarchy is well-motivated
Comprehensive evaluation: 18 state-of-the-art MLLMs tested, human baseline established, both thinking-enabled and non-thinking models covered

Strong empirical insights: Figure 5 convincingly shows extended thinking provides 9% improvement on VIDEOREASONBENCH vs <2.5% on existing benchmarks; Table 3 demonstrates this benchmark has 55% vision reliance vs 1-7% for others
High reproducibility: semi-automatic generation pipeline, detailed templates, inference configs documented, code/data promised
Effective ablations and analysis: vid2txt experiments isolate temporal perception bottleneck, case studies illustrate failure modes, robustness checks confirm evaluation stability
Well-written and clearly presented with effective figures communicating key insights
weaknesses: Modest dataset scale: 240 videos and 1,440 questions is relatively small by current benchmarking standards; potential vulnerability to overfitting

Narrow scope of reasoning tasks: all tasks involve deterministic state tracking in discrete domains; lacks causal reasoning, intent understanding, multi-agent scenarios, and other reasoning types central to video understanding

Artificial/controlled domain limitations: 'clean' videos lack real-world challenges (motion blur, occlusion, lighting); gap between synthetic and natural videos unexplored; limits real-world applicability

Question design concerns: templates appear highly formulaic with limited semantic variation; vid2txt baseline's dramatic improvements (e.g., 11.5%→69.4%) suggest pattern matching rather than true vision reasoning

Evaluation gaps: LLM-based judging has documented faithfulness issues; Predict Operation tasks lack ground-truth answers and rely on state simulation vulnerable to edge cases; only 5 models in correlation validation (Table 9)

Incomplete analysis: no inter-annotator agreement for human baseline; minimal error categorization beyond two failure modes; limited breakdown of performance by video type; missing discussion of why temporal reveal timing has dramatic effects
Limited immediate impact: paper is descriptive (benchmark + evaluation) without proposing solutions for improving model performance or advancing video reasoning capabilities
Generalization concerns: synthetic domain-specific nature limits evidence that insights transfer to natural video understanding or broader video reasoning capabilities

strengths: Clear problem identification: paper identifies genuine gap in existing video benchmarks lacking reasoning depth for extended CoT
Systematic benchmark design: elegant formalization of videos as state transitions with controlled complexity parameters
Comprehensive evaluation: 18 SOTAs evaluated with multi-faceted analysis (thinking budget, vision reliance, complexity scaling)
Strong empirical findings: clear demonstration that thinking helps more on this benchmark (~9%) than existing ones (<2.5%)
Reproducibility: extensive prompts, templates, evaluation procedures, and promised code/data release
weaknesses: Critical contradiction: paper claims 'vision-centric' reasoning but vid2txt experiments show 45-58 point improvements with text alone (69.4% for Seed1.5-VL, 72.2% for Gemini-2.5-Flash), proving models solve ~70% via language reasoning without visual content
Limited technical novelty: core idea (track latent states through operations) is straightforward; six categories are mechanical template variations without conceptual innovation
Synthetic/controlled videos severely limit applicability: no motion blur, occlusion, lighting variation, or real-world perceptual challenges; unclear if results transfer to realistic scenarios
Small dataset: 240 videos/1,440 questions (≈40 examples per skill×category); high variance risk and overfitting concern for future work
Weak human baseline validation: only 3 annotators, no inter-annotator agreement metrics reported, 223.2 sec/question raises design concerns, highly skewed accuracy (87.5% vs 42.5%)
LLM-based evaluation introduces noise: using Qwen2.5-72B as judge for correctness is indirect; structured output evaluation via LLM extraction + simulation is fragile
State reveal timing asymmetry unexplained: dramatic performance drops when state revealed at end (66.9%→45.1%) suggests unequal task variants and tests backward rather than forward reasoning
Weak generalization evidence: Table 9 correlation with LMArena uses only 5 cherry-picked data points; cannot validate benchmark quality or generalizability
Missing critical ablations: no simple baseline solvers, limited analysis of failure modes, no cross-category generalization study, no prompt engineering ablation
Overclaimed significance: framing as addressing major video understanding gap is overstated given synthetic nature, small scope, and contradiction in vision-centric claim

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies gap in existing benchmarks that require reasoning depth but don't benefit from extended CoT
Elegant task formulation: principled state-transition framework with three-level reasoning hierarchy and six diverse demonstration types
Comprehensive evaluation: 18 models (efficient, flagship, proprietary) with thorough ablations on thinking budget, vision reliance, and complexity scaling
Rigorous analysis: LLM-based evaluation validated across paraphrasing and multiple judges; correlation with LMArena; concrete case studies; human baseline at 73.8%
High-quality presentation: clear writing, effective figures, extensive appendices with reproducibility resources and implementation details

Actionable insights: demonstration that CoT reasoning is essential for VRB (~9% improvement) but offers minimal gains on existing benchmarks (~2.5%), challenging generalizability of test-time scaling claims
Strong vision-reliance validation: 55% performance drop when removing 50% of video vs. ≤7% on existing benchmarks, confirming benchmark design
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale: 1,440 questions/240 videos with equal distribution yields only ~40 examples per category-question type pair; no confidence intervals or significance tests; per-category conclusions underpowered

LLM-based evaluation methodology concerns: unknown alignment between LLM judge and human understanding of complex spatial/logical reasoning; Predict Operation relies on state simulation rather than reasoning verification; no inter-annotator agreement metrics for human baseline

Synthetic/controlled videos: no occlusion, motion blur, lighting variation; dramatic vid2txt jumps (e.g., Seed1.5-VL 11.5%→69.4%) suggest visual perception is bottleneck; limits generalization claims to naturalistic scenarios

Template-based question generation: systematically limited diversity; hand-crafted automatic answers may miss reasoning errors not propagating to incorrect final state; no ablation on formulation diversity
Limited actionability: identifies problems but proposes no solutions for improving performance; primarily diagnostic rather than prescriptive; no investigation of training strategies
Incomplete concurrent work comparison: VCR-Bench and MINERVA (which evaluate reasoning process correctness) dismissed without detailed comparison; design choice unjustified

Insufficient error analysis: unclear why Gemini-2.5-Pro achieves only 56% vs. 73.8% human; remaining gap attribution (visual vs. reasoning) incompletely explored; no granular error breakdown per reasoning level
Potential frontier model bias: Gemini-2.5-Pro significantly outperforms all others; unclear if true capability or benchmark overfitting; model scaling insights limited and non-uniform
